awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of A Sustainable Approach for Ammonia Fertilizer
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this I-Corps project is based on the development of catalysts and electrochemical reactors to convert nitrogen feedstocks into nitrogenous fertilizers, which are valuable commodities. Current production methods utilize the Haber-Bosch process, which requires extreme pressures and temperatures, consuming approximately 2% of the world’s energy supply and emitting nearly 2% of total greenhouse gas emissions globally. This innovative production method could reduce energy input by 30%, lower carbon intensity by more than 90%, and decrease the cost of production by at least 40% compared to the baseline technology. This process could provide end-users such as farmers, meatpacking plants, and wastewater treatment facilities with an on-site production method for cheaper, more efficient, and more sustainable fertilizer production.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. The solution is based on the development of catalysts and electrochemical reactors that convert nitrogen feedstocks into nitrogenous fertilizers, which are valuable commodities. This technology can potentially generate ammonia fertilizer with an energy input 25-40% below the energy input of the state-of-the-art process (i.e., Haber-Bosch Process) with zero carbon dioxide emissions. This technology utilizes state-of-the-art single-atom catalysts (SACs) and nanoparticles to directly generate nitrogenous fertilizers from abundant nitrogen sources. The technology develops materials and systems that are affordable and energy-efficient compared to traditional fossil fuel-based methods. By focusing on electrifying and reducing emissions in nitrogen fertilizer production, the technology can later be fully adopted for industrial use. This approach will help lower carbon emissions and energy use in the chemical industry.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF I-Corps project evaluated the commercial potential of a decentralized electrochemical technology that converts nitrogen-containing waste streams into ammonia and other fertilizer products. The technology is intended to address two connected challenges: nitrogen pollution from agricultural and industrial wastewater and the dependence of fertilizer production on large, centralized, energy-intensive facilities.

The project focused on understanding whether the technology addresses a meaningful customer need and what technical, economic, and operational requirements must be met for practical adoption. The team conducted more than 140 interviews with stakeholders from agriculture, dairy operations, fertilizer production, wastewater treatment, resource recovery, electrochemical systems, and related industries. These discussions helped identify potential customers, partners, early adopters, competing approaches, regulatory considerations, and barriers to implementation. 

A key finding was that the strongest value proposition extends beyond producing ammonia as a commodity. Potential users were particularly interested in systems that could combine wastewater treatment, nitrogen removal, nutrient recovery, and on-site fertilizer production. Dairy farms and other agricultural operations emerged as promising early markets because they face significant costs and operational challenges associated with manure lagoons, nutrient management, hauling, land application, water use, and fertilizer purchasing. The project therefore refined the commercialization strategy toward modular systems that can be installed where nitrogen-rich waste streams are already generated.

The project also clarified the technical requirements needed for successful deployment. These include reliable operation with complex and variable wastewater, low energy consumption, high nitrogen-conversion efficiency, long system lifetime, limited maintenance, and compatibility with existing agricultural and wastewater infrastructure. Related technical studies improved understanding of electrochemical reaction conditions, reactor design, mass transport, and energy efficiency. One reactor-design study indicated that a multi-electrode configuration could reduce modeled energy consumption by approximately 22 percent compared with a conventional flow-cell design.

The award-supported translation effort contributed to three peer-reviewed journal articles and three conference presentations. These products shared findings on electrochemical wastewater treatment, nitrogen recovery, decentralized ammonia production, pulsed nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, and energy-efficient electrochemical reactor design.

The project also strengthened the pathway for technology transfer. Two patent applications were filed: “Methods for Formation of Ammonia Using Diverse Nitrogen-Based Feedstocks” and “Apparatus for Formation of Ammonia Using Diverse Nitrogen-Based Feedstocks.” The team further developed NitroCat Energies, Inc. as a potential vehicle for advancing the technology toward pilot demonstrations, strategic partnerships, licensing, and commercialization.

Two Ph.D. students received interdisciplinary training through the project. They gained experience in customer discovery, market analysis, stakeholder communication, intellectual-property awareness, business-model development, scientific publishing, and technology translation. These experiences prepared them to connect laboratory research with real-world environmental, economic, and societal needs.

The broader potential impacts include improved water quality, reduced nutrient pollution, more resilient fertilizer supply chains, reduced transportation requirements, and new economic opportunities for agricultural and rural communities. Overall, the project demonstrated a credible pathway for translating electrochemical nitrogen recovery from academic research toward practical use, while identifying the technical validation and pilot-scale testing still needed for commercial deployment.
